items.proposed_text: "Linked to" is not "causes". Two things can go together without one causing the other. People who use a drug may differ in other ways too. We say "causes" only when the studies can show it. In one study, a third of press releases on such links made them sound more like causes.
items.why: The first two sentences rest on Hill (a clear association beyond chance still has to be weighed against other explanations; people who smoke may differ in exercise or diet), Cohen (unrelated problems appear together among people in treatment), Sumner (a correlation can run either way or come from a third factor) and Robins 1975 and 1993 (drug use went with later problems, but earlier factors may have caused both; heroin's extra problems vanished once behaviour before service and the number of other drugs were held constant). The third sentence is the site's rule; Hill qualifies it: no single feature proves a cause and none is required, so 'show' means making a cause the most likely explanation, which observational evidence can sometimes do. The fourth sentence rests on no paper here: Hill says only that occupational medicine more often than not starts from observed associations. The proposed sentence rests on Sumner (33 in 100 press releases, 39 in 100 news stories). Sumner's scale itself rates 'linked to' as ambiguous wording, which is why the page has to say what the site means by it. If a sentence about the site's own answers is kept instead, the claim files support 'Few of our answers say "causes"' (editors' count of data/claims/*.json, 26 November 2026: 36 of 412 claims worded 'increases' or 'reduces', none 'causes'; 176 worded as associations, the commonest), not 'most'.

items.proposed_text: Who was studied? People in treatment, in prison or in hospital are not everyone who uses a drug.
items.why: Cohen argue, with a constructed example rather than data, that people met in treatment on any day over-represent long-lasting problems, that people who recover without treatment tend to do better, and that findings from a service apply to people seen in similar services. Robins gives real numbers: of men addicted in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in the first year home and 12 in 100 within three years, against about two-thirds of young men treated at Lexington re-addicted within six months, and she concludes that addiction looks very different in a general population than in treated cases (while calling Vietnam's conditions unprecedented). Robins 1975 names 'treated or arrested' people as the basis of earlier studies; no paper here names prison, and arrest is the nearest. Gigerenzer: ask whether a risk comes from studies of people like you.

items.proposed_text: Were they tested before they started? If not, a difference may have been there before the drug.
items.why: Hill's temporality asks which came first and whether the people who chose an exposure were already more liable. Robins 1975: drug use went with later problems, but factors before the drug use may have led to both. Robins 1993 gives a worked case: heroin went with more problems than amphetamines or barbiturates, but not once behaviour problems before service and the number of other drugs were held constant; and the men who went on to use narcotics already differed before service (27 in 100 of those with no earlier drug use used narcotics in Vietnam, against 100 in 100 of those with four or more kinds). Caveat for the editor: Robins's 'before' information was mostly asked after return, so no paper here actually tested people before first use; a prospective cohort measured before first use would be the stronger source.

items.proposed_text: How much, how often, and how? One dose in a lab is not the same as using every day.
items.why: That amount and frequency change what a finding means is supported: Hill's biological gradient (a risk that rises with amount strengthens a causal reading; exposure is often hard to measure) and Robins 1993 (re-addiction after Vietnam was confined to men who used heroin regularly, about half of whom were re-addicted, by the text and Figure 6 read approximately). The second sentence, one laboratory dose against daily use, rests on no paper here. Text kept as it is until a source is added. Kind of source: studies giving the same drug once and repeatedly (tolerance), or a methods review of how laboratory doses, settings and volunteers differ from use outside the laboratory; on the site, the drug's checked tolerance answer where one exists.

items.site_text: How big is the difference? "Significant" means probably not chance. It does not mean big. A group can score a bit lower on average while almost everyone in it scores in the normal range.

items.proposed_text: How big is the difference? "Significant" does not mean proven, and it does not mean big. With enough people, even a tiny difference can be "significant". And "not significant" does not mean "no difference".
items.why: 'Probably not chance' is the reading the ASA statement rules out (principle 2), Gigerenzer count reading a p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is correct among textbook errors, and in Ioannidis's model a result with P < 0.05 is more likely false than true whenever power times the pre-study odds is below 0.05; when psychology studies were repeated once, 35 of 97 significant results were significant again. Hill used the loose words too, but added that only repetition may tell chance from a real effect. 'Not big' rests on principle 5, Hill and Ioannidis (large studies can make trivial effects significant); the converse error on Hill, principle 6 and Boutron (10 of 72 trial abstracts claimed equivalence from non-significant results). The normal-range sentence rests on no paper here: it states a possibility, not a finding. If kept, it needs its own anchor; the site's checked claim cl_meth_cognition_normal_range says a group average in the normal range does not mean every person is (in two studies about a quarter to a third of people who used meth met an impairment definition), so 'most' would fit better than 'almost everyone'.

items.proposed_text: Out of how many? "Twice the risk" can mean 2 in 100 instead of 1 in 100, or 2 in a million instead of 1 in a million.
items.why: Gigerenzer: a 1995 warning that a pill doubled ('100%') the risk of blood clots rested on about 1 against 2 in 7,000 women; relative changes look big when the base rate is low; a relative change can be worked out from absolute numbers but not the reverse; and, citing other studies, 45 in 100 press releases gave relative risks without base rates and 68 in 100 of 222 journal articles gave no absolute risks in the abstract. The site's own example is arithmetic. Two qualifications, not contradictions: Hill (ratios are the better guide to whether something is a cause; absolute differences tell how many extra cases) and Gigerenzer (without a comparison, absolute numbers can make an important effect look negligible).

items.proposed_text: Did another team find the same? One study is a lead, not a fact.
items.why: Open Science Collaboration: when 100 psychology studies were repeated once by other teams, 35 of 97 significant results were significant again (36 in 100), effects were about half as large, and the authors conclude that a single study almost never settles a question. Ioannidis calls conclusive claims from one significant study ill-founded and asks for the totality of evidence; the ASA statement adds that selective reporting fills the literature with significant results. Qualifications: a failed repetition does not prove the original false (OSC); repeating the same flawed design repeats its error, results reached in different ways count more, and a single unrepeatable observation can occasionally convince (Hill). Optional, on Hill's point: 'Did another team find the same, another way?'

items.proposed_text: Does the summary say more than the data? Headlines often do. Our study cards note the gap.
items.why: Sumner coded the title and first two sentences of press releases and news stories against the journal article (UK universities, 2011): press releases gave stronger advice in 40 in 100, more causal wording in 33 in 100 and stretched animal or cell results to humans in 36 in 100; news stories gave stronger advice in 36 in 100 and more causal wording in 39 in 100, mostly when their press release already had. Boutron: of 72 trial reports with non-significant main results, 42 abstract conclusions and 13 titles put a favourable spin on them. Gigerenzer, citing others: 77 in 100 press releases noted no limitations. Limits: health research in general, not drug research; Sumner's baseline is the journal article, which may itself overstate. 'Our study cards note the gap' is a fact about the site (every card has an interpretation-gap field, METHODS §5.1), not a finding.
